title: I've studied nuclear war for 15 years - you should be worried
summary: Author of a nuclear-war scenario book on how fast a nuclear exchange unfolds, launch on warning, weak missile defence and nuclear winter.

assertions.quote: We are closer to nuclear Armageddon than we have ever been since the Cuban missile crisis and that is terrifying.

verdicts.note: The Doomsday Clock is at its closest ever and arms control has lapsed, but few experts rate today's risk above the worst Cold War crises.

The Bulletin's closest-ever Clock and its account of three nuclear-shadowed conflicts in 2025 point to elevated risk, but the composite Clock does not show nuclear risk exceeds the Cuban Missile Crisis.

assertions.quote: This launch was mistaken by an early warning system in Russia for an ICBM launch.

verdicts.note: A linked Metaculus forecast gives 20% that the first nuclear detonation by 2050 is inadvertent (launched on a mistaken belief of being under attack), so forecasters see miscalculation as a real pathway.

FRI's median expert put an inadvertent nuclear detonation (launched on a false belief of being attacked) by 2030 at 1.3% and an accidental one at 1% (superforecasters 0.1% and 0.05%), and said an inadvertent one would triple catastrophe risk.

The paper lays out accidental and inadvertent routes to US-Russia nuclear war, noting that weather, a faulty chip, animals and misloaded training tapes have all been mistaken for attack indicators while both sides stay ready to launch on warning.

RAND judges that inadvertent strikes or misread signals between Russia and NATO could begin spirals ending in nuclear use, a risk that 'hangs over any instance of direct conflict between nuclear-armed states'.

US intelligence names an escalatory spiral in an ongoing or new conflict, including nuclear exchanges, as Russia's most dangerous threat, which supports escalation through miscalculation but does not address pure accidents.

RAND notes the tension between launch-under-attack postures and the chance of accident, citing the 1983 Soviet early-warning malfunction that 'detected' a nonexistent US attack and could have prompted retaliation against a phantom assault.

SIPRI cites the 1983 Petrov incident, a malfunction in the Soviet Oko early-warning system that falsely showed a US ICBM attack, and warns more automation in warning and command systems could raise the risk of inadvertent nuclear use.
A Metaculus question shown beside this one puts 20% on the first nuclear detonation by 2050 being inadvertent (24 forecasters), treating accidental use as a real possibility; a sidebar figure only.

assertions.quote: the president has sole launch authority. He does not need to ask anyone.

verdicts.note: US command and control gives the president sole authority to order nuclear use without the consent of Congress or the cabinet.

assertions.quote: Launch on warning is reckless and dangerous and should be changed.

verdicts.note: Short decision times raise the risk of acting on a false alarm, though no false alarm has yet led to a launch.

Launch on warning acts on a single sensor family and the paper calls it 'more error-prone' than launch under attack, which needs confirmation from both satellite and radar; the model assumes both sides shift to it in crises.

RAND says Russia's shift to launching during an attack instead of riding it out amounts to a launch-under-attack posture that pressures leaders to launch first in a crisis, increasing the chances of accidental escalation.

SIPRI calls launch-on-warning or launch-under-attack postures destabilizing and warns any technical glitch, false alarm or algorithmic error could trigger catastrophic escalation, while states hold to these postures more firmly.

assertions.quote: There are a grand total of 44 interceptor missiles in the US arsenal.

verdicts.note: US homeland defence has 44 ground-based interceptors designed against a few North Korean missiles, not a Russian salvo.
The Bulletin states missile defence systems are at best only partially effective, even with Golden Dome's space-based interceptors.

assertions.quote: Nuclear war followed by nuclear winter will send man back to its hunter gatherer origins.

verdicts.note: XPT forecasters saw nuclear winter as the only plausible route to extinction from nuclear war but flagged substantial scientific uncertainty, and put nuclear extinction by 2100 at 0.074% (superforecasters) to 0.55% (experts).

assertions.quote: one to two billion people would die after a war between India and Pakistan of starvation.

verdicts.note: Climate models project large crop losses from such a war, but soot estimates and outcomes are contested.
XPT forecasters judged that a regional exchange such as India-Pakistan would not kill more than 10% of humanity, which limits the scale claimed but does not rule out a global famine.

assertions.quote: for the first time since the cold war ended, we have a Russian president who is actually has mentioned the possibility of nuclear use.

verdicts.note: SIPRI records that Russia revised its doctrine in November 2024 to claim the right to use nuclear weapons against aggression by a non-nuclear state supported by a nuclear-armed state.
